before.label: Interpretive historical sociology
before.description: Interpretive understanding, ideal types, legitimate domination, rationalization, and comparative histories of capitalism and religion. Meaningful interpretation requires causal evidence. Historical questions are selected through cultural concerns, while their answers remain open to public assessment; editorial and translational mediation shape later readings.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Max Weber (1864–1920), The Protestant Ethic (1904–05). Later modernization theory selectively appropriates Weber; his own view of modernity is more ambivalent.

before.scope_note: Interpretive sociology, capitalist development, and theories of domination travel through different readers and intermediaries. Ideal types are analytical constructions, not averages or stages every society must traverse. Marianne Weber contributes independent legal-historical research and posthumous editing; Parsons and Lipset make particular later uses. Weber’s qualified defense of materialist inquiry prevents a simple Marx-versus-ideas binary.

strands.title: Meaning and causal evidence
strands.focus: A plausible interpretation of motives is a hypothesis requiring evidence. Understanding does not demand personal empathy, and rational idealization is not a claim that people always act rationally.

strands.title: Ideal types and collective action
strands.focus: Types clarify comparison without serving as averages or compulsory stages. States and organizations matter through actions and meaningful orientations; methodological individualism does not entail individualistic political values.

strands.title: Value relevance and public validity
strands.focus: Cultural concerns select questions; this does not make the validity of answers arbitrary. General regularities help explain particular histories but cannot alone supply a complete account of a specific constellation.

strands.title: Religious conduct and capitalist constraints
strands.focus: The Protestant Ethic conclusion considers ascetic conduct and institutions whose operation outlives religious motivations. It calls for further inquiry into reciprocal conditions and rejects one-sided spiritual causation.
strands.works: Protestant Ethic, printed 119–125 in Parsons translation

strands.title: Legal history and editorial mediation
strands.focus: Marianne Weber’s independent inquiry into women’s legal position belongs alongside her posthumous editing and biography. The unity and arrangement of Economy and Society remain questions in reception.
strands.works: Ehefrau und Mutter (1907); posthumous editions (1921–22); Lebensbild (1926)

strands.title: Different comparative and institutional receptions
strands.focus: Parsons’s translation and institutional comparison, Lipset’s democracy analysis and Bendix’s authority/citizenship inquiry select different resources. No single modernization reading exhausts Weber.

before.label: Historical economics
before.description: Historical economists investigate the changing institutions and conditions within which economic claims hold. German programmes, British disciplinary formation, and empirical price research overlap but differ. Their debates concern how to combine explanation and historical evidence: Toynbee values conditional deduction, while Schmoller disputes Menger’s account of abstraction.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Gustav Schmoller; William Ashley; William Cunningham; Arnold Toynbee. Thorold Rogers supplies a related empirical tradition in prices and wages. Contextual readings now distinguish Roscher’s 1843 programme, Schmoller’s 1883 methodological review, Cunningham’s textbook, Ashley’s medieval studies, Toynbee’s lectures, Rogers’s wage research and Menger’s criticism.

after.label: Historical economics
after.description: Historical economists investigate the changing institutions and conditions within which economic claims hold. German programmes, British disciplinary formation, and empirical price research overlap but differ. Their debates concern how to combine explanation and historical evidence: Toynbee values conditional deduction, while Schmoller disputes Menger’s account of abstraction. Earlier disputes also separate Jones’s comparative tenures, Roscher’s contextual programme, Hildebrand’s critique of opposed specialization schemes and Knies’s objections to Roscher’s method. Leslie’s account emphasizes policy differences within historical inquiry.

after.scope_note: German historical economics, British institutional history, and empirical price studies overlap without forming one school. Roscher’s earlier programme and Schmoller’s generation differ. Menger is shown as a critic, and Toynbee explicitly rejects exclusive reliance on historical investigation. National and civilizational categories in these texts are historical claims to examine, not a globally representative framework. Jones’s providential harmony and Hildebrand’s national-capacity judgments are not adopted as findings.

strands.title: Tenures and the limits of general rent theory
strands.focus: Jones grounds comparison in different arrangements between owners and cultivators; his social-harmony conclusions remain contestable.

strands.title: Historical inquiry and policy plurality
strands.focus: Leslie describes conservative and liberal positions within German historical inquiry; Hildebrand questions opposing models of specialization. Neither yields one policy for every historical economist.

strands.title: Disagreement within historical economics
strands.focus: Knies argues that Roscher’s programme confuses method with its subject and intended results. Their shared historical commitments do not settle how explanation should work.

strands.title: Selective reception and disciplinary argument
strands.focus: Ashley invokes Jones and Leslie in defending economic history; Weber uses Knies to isolate logical problems. These are distinct acts of reception.

Jones limits Ricardian rent theory to particular tenures and proposes comparative observation; his forecast of harmonious class interests and providential, civilizational assumptions remain attributed claims. Weber explicitly selects logical problems rather than offering a complete historical assessment of Knies; he questions the derivation of method from a science’s assigned subject matter. Later argument and1906continuation unread. Reception/edition history in his opening is his account, not an independent reception census.

outcomes.finding: Jones, Leslie, Hildebrand and Knies receive distinct contexts grounded in their primary texts. Jones compares tenures; Leslie mediates and criticizes German writing; Hildebrand contests opposing specialization schemes; Knies questions Roscher’s method. Ashley1893 supplies particular Jones/Leslie reception, Leslie recommends Knies, Knies critically receives Hildebrand, and Weber’s opening supplies a later methodological intervention.
outcomes.research_limit: Selected prefaces, one complete Leslie article and bounded original passages, not complete books or an exhaustive reception history. Leslie1876article inaccessible after web and normal/escalated curl attempts. Jones’s Literary Remains as quoted by Ashley was not separately collated. Knies1883revision and Weber’s later argument unread. Priority allegations and portraits of opponents remain attributed.

outcomes.finding: Roscher1843preface now directly supports the contextual programme and qualified use of Ricardo; his roster context retains its previous wording and adds this substance and citation. Leslie’s policy plurality, Hildebrand’s critique of national/international specialization and Knies’s internal objections prevent a unitary historical-school account.
